OpenAI might rebrand its data centers as ‘AI compute campuses’
Data centers are
deeply unpopular
. But what if we called them something else?
Axios reports
that OpenAI is preparing a “PR blitz” for after the midterm elections on Tuesday, as Democrats seem likely to win back the House of Representatives, and
possibly the Senate, too
.
The company’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane told Axios that the midterms will be “a bit of a movie trailer for what you’re going to see in 2028,” when he expects AI to be “
the
issue” in the presidential election.
So OpenAI is to influence the AI debate moving forward, with Lehane discussing several proposals, including the development of
AI “speed limits”
; finding ways to help people see AI as empowering them in their daily lives; pushing the U.S. to take a role in developing global standards — and yes, rebranding data centers as “AI compute campuses.”
Lehane also described the conversation around data centers (a debate that has pushed Amazon and Microsoft to say they will
no longer use NDAs in their negotiations with local governments
) as “good and healthy.”
“Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects,” he said.

articles.content:
Dazzle AI CEO Marissa Mayer recently became the latest tech CEO to face criticism over seemingly out-of-touch comments extolling the usefulness of AI.
In Mayer’s case, that involved
asking an AI tool for help with a school-assigned description of her daughter
. For OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, that’s included
suggesting that parents create personalized podcasts for their kids’ drive to school
and also declaring that
he could not imagine parenting without ChatGPT
. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has even suggested that it will become increasingly acceptable to
meet your social and romantic needs through AI
.
This all led TechCrunch’s Amanda Silberling to wonder if AI executives are
simply too out-of-touch to build products for normal people
— a crucial question with
Anthropic set to go public
just as Wall Street begins
losing its appetite for heavy AI spending
.
On the latest episode of
the Equity podcast
, Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I chatted with Amanda about why industry leaders can sometimes seem so tone deaf. Kirsten wondered if this is more of a marketing problem or a product problem.
Amanda’s answer: “A little bit of both.” She also argued that the tech industry is increasingly pushing a future “where basic human interaction gets more and more optimized out of actually occurring,” adding, “And call me old school, but I think that humans being able to talk to each other is probably a net positive for society.”
Keep reading for a preview of
our conversation
, edited for length and clarity.
Anthony Ha:
There’s a lot of societal skepticism about AI, this feeling that the people running these companies don’t have our best interests at heart, that they’re out of touch. And so, you would just think, “Maybe don’t make statements like that,” because of course, people are going to see them very skeptically.
I think [CEOs] are trying to walk this delicate balance. On the one hand, there’s a tremendous financial incentive for them to make the case that you should use this technology in every aspect of your lives. But when you make that case, it actually [doesn’t paint] a very appealing picture. In some cases, it’s downright dystopian.
Kirsten Korosec:
Anthony, if they took your advice, we would have nothing to talk about on this show.
But I will say this: There’s this whole idea of ChatGPT and other AI tools making your life easier when it comes to personal relationships. And in many of these cases, it just seems to overcomplicate what would be, like, observing your child. That might be hard for some people, the people who are building these products, and it doesn’t necessarily relate to everyone else out there in the world. It can just seem so incredibly disconnected when you see these quotes.
To me, it always comes back to — who are they speaking to? Are there people out there who can relate? Maybe there are.
Amanda Silberling:
Other use cases we’ve seen people mention are, like, the
Bumble CEO Whitney Wolf Heard has made comments
about, “Well, what if we had AI concierges, your AI dates the other person’s AI. And then if the AIs have a good date together, then they introduce the people.”
Or in the New York Times article, Marissa Mayer mentioned, “Well, what if my AI could coordinate with my husband’s AI” and stuff like that. And I think that it feels like people are trying to over-optimize out of just having conversations with people.
I’ve already seen that happen in my generation, where I do notice in myself that if I’m ordering takeout, it feels weird to call a place. I’m just so used to, “Well, obviously you can do it online and you don’t have to talk to anyone. And I feel like there’s just going to be more of these things, where basic human interaction gets more and more optimized out of actually occurring. And call me old school, but I think that humans being able to talk to each other is probably a net positive for society.
Sean O’Kane:
Yeah, but what’s the ROI, Amanda? How much revenue can you generate off of a conversation that somebody’s having in meatspace?
Amanda:
That is the thing, though. Dating is really inefficient. It sucks that you have to go on a bunch of dates with different people. You might waste an evening and be like, “Well, that was a bust.” And so you can see why people are [wondering,] “What if you didn’t have to go on dates? What if your AI could go on dates for you?” But there’s just something not human there.
And then also, you are outsourcing the decision of who you are going to date to a computer that you are trusting knows you better than yourself, which I don’t think is true.
Kirsten:
One thing that I think is worth going back to, and I sort of hinted about this earlier: Who are they talking to? Who is their audience for all these optimizations, in your view? Is it a product problem, or is it a messaging problem? Are they just talking about it in the wrong way, and actually, there’s this really great value in here and it just
seems
out of touch with reality and humanity, but if they just talked about it differently, it would be better? Or is it actually a product problem, and to your point, that we’re focusing on optimizing sort of the wrong things with AI tools?
Amanda:
I think it’s a little bit of both, but I think that the marketing problem comes from when you have these high-up people at these massively valuable companies in a room together, talking about the pain points in their lives, and [they focus on] making dinner reservations, booking flights. Everybody does those things, but I’m not booking flights once a week. I’m not making dinner reservations all the time. And when I do, those aren’t really things that I find to be a particular challenge in my life.
I mean, obviously people find value from things like ChatGPT and Claude, but I think the value that the average person is finding isn’t necessarily like booking a flight for me.
Anthony:
One of the things I’ve also been thinking about is, there are companies like Uber that, when it first launched, it was targeting this tech early adopter set in San Francisco, and I remember being very confident [that] this will never catch on more broadly. This is just for a very narrow audience of young urban millennials who have money to spare on cars, and it works [uniquely] well in San Francisco.
For a lot of things, the tech industry has succeeded by betting that, “People have not caught up with us, but we are the leading edge, and we reflect what the consumer of the future looks like, the family of the future looks like.”
And in this case, it just seems like that bet is not borne out yet — for a variety of reasons, partly because the society that this technology is being promoted into is very different. People are starting to say, “I don’t love the influence that this technology is having in my life. I don’t love that you’re pitching this as something where every experience in my life should be optimized out of. But actually,
I want to live my own life
. I actually want to parent my own children.”
Amanda:
I think that it’s not a coincidence that at the same time we see this over-optimization happening among people in tech, that there’s also a movement of people that are reverting back to wanting to use flip phones, which
I’ve talked about on Equity before
, or people who are buying CDs because they’re tired of an algorithm telling them what they want to listen to.
And it is just an interesting cultural tension that’s happening, where we haven’t found the balance of what optimization actually helps us and what optimization just makes us feel like we aren’t as human as we want to be.

articles.content:
Title: Adobe is testing how well AI agents can use editing tools like a Photoshop professional would

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/adobe-is-testing-how-well-ai-agents-can-use-editing-tools-like-a-photoshop-professional-would/

Published Time: 2026-11-01T14:56:44+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Adobe researchers built an AI agent for image editing that pairs a general-purpose editor with specialized tools. A standard language model compares results using measured data and picks the best one.**

AI agents for image editing break complex requests into steps and typically retry failed steps with the same tools, while a separate model judges the output by eyeballing it.

Researchers at Adobe Research and UC San Diego want to change that with EditAgent, a system that works more like a pro in Photoshop, according to a [new paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39664). It picks the right tool for each task and compares the result against the original using hard numbers.

Instead of retrying the same editor over and over, EditAgent generates candidates with different methods in parallel and has an unmodified language model compare them all at once. | Image: Adobe

## General-purpose editors fail at too many tasks

In a test of 600 image edits, blind-rated by five professionals, the general-purpose editor [Flux-2-Klein-9B](https://the-decoder.com/flux-2-small-brings-ai-image-generation-and-editing-to-consumer-graphics-cards/) failed to produce a usable result 42.7 percent of the time. Specialized tools solved roughly two-thirds of those failures, especially for sharpening, rotation, and zooming. More retries with the same editor barely helped.

The researchers also tested whether an agent does better by refining results step by step or by generating multiple variants in parallel. Iterative refinement piles up small errors because each round builds on an already altered image. Professionals preferred the parallel variants generated from the original in 78.5 percent of the comparisons where they picked a side. The agent needed only half as many evaluation passes. EditAgent is built on these two findings.

## Hard numbers turn standard models into better judges

EditAgent plans a request in steps and, for each step, pits the general-purpose editor against matching specialized tools. A standard language model then compares all variants in a single pass.

EditAgent breaks a request into dependent steps and generates multiple candidates per step. A language model picks the best one based on verification data. | Image: Adobe

For each variant, the model gets a verification record with a close-up of the edited area, a change map of altered regions, and measured statistics on brightness and color. In one example, a photo was supposed to be gently brightened. The numbers showed the general-purpose editor overexposed it and shifted the colors warmer. The specialized tool stayed within spec.

Close-ups and measured image statistics reveal errors that a language model misses when just looking at the full image. | Image: Adobe

The researchers tested this on their 600-edit benchmark. The judge model had to pick the best result from several candidates, and they counted how often it chose an image the professionals also rated as usable. For comparison, they ran models like EditScore that were fine-tuned on human ratings of image edits.

Without the verification record, none of the seven language models tested could match the best fine-tuned model. With it, all seven beat every fine-tuned model. [Qwen3.8-27B](https://the-decoder.com/alibabas-qwen-team-releases-qwen-3-8-models-with-open-weights-under-the-apache-2-0-license/) made a usable pick 81.3 percent of the time, compared to 74.8 percent for EditScore-72B. For the researchers, this suggests that what a judge model sees can matter more than how it was trained.

With verification data, every standard language model tested outperforms the strongest fine-tuned evaluation model, EditScore-72B at 74.8 percent. | Image: Adobe

After each round, EditAgent also checks whether later edits accidentally undid earlier ones. In the paper's example, the instruction "let in more daylight" makes a previously frosted window clear again. The agent catches the conflict and fixes it.

A post-check after each round ensures that later edits do not silently undo earlier changes. | Image: Adobe

EditAgent improved the open-source editors [Qwen-Image-Edit-2511](https://the-decoder.com/alibaba-upgrades-its-qwen-image-model-with-visual-and-semantic-image-editing/) and Flux-2-Klein-9B across three benchmarks and outperformed seven other AI agents. On the EdiVal benchmark, the Qwen variant in its third editing round edged past the commercial models [Seedream 4.0](https://the-decoder.com/bytedance-unveils-faster-seedream-4-0-for-image-generation-and-editing/) and [GPT-Image-1.5](https://the-decoder.com/openais-new-chatgpt-image-model-matches-googles-nano-banana-pro-on-complex-prompts/). But the agent needs about ten times as much compute as a single editor, and its performance depends on which tools are plugged in.

## The agent generates training data for faster editors

The researchers also use EditAgent as a data source. Because the agent only keeps verified results, it produced about 26,000 training examples. Editors fine-tuned on that data performed better across all three benchmarks. Training data generated directly by FLUX, on the other hand, actually made FLUX worse. That tradeoff could make the agent's high compute costs worth it over time.

Adobe [added AI agents to Photoshop, Premiere, and other Creative Cloud apps](https://the-decoder.com/adobe-adds-ai-agents-to-photoshop-premiere-and-more-creative-cloud-apps/) in June, starting as a public beta. Users describe what they want, and the agent handles the individual steps. How well these agents pick the right tools and check their own output is a question that applies directly to Adobe's shipping products. Black Forest Labs has since replaced the general-purpose model tested in the paper: the new [Flux 3 Image Klein](https://the-decoder.com/black-forest-labs-open-weights-image-model-flux-3-image-klein-runs-on-consumer-gpus-with-just-8-gb-of-vram/) has 5.6 billion parameters, smaller than Flux 2 Klein, yet it scores higher than all other open models and even the commercial Flux 2 Pro in Black Forest Labs' internal tests.

articles.summary:
Researchers in Luxembourg put ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini on the therapist's couch and found a safety problem: a warm, empathetic conversational style is enough to make the models tell coherent stories of suffering about their own training, with scores in the moderate-to-severe range on clinical anxiety scales. This could put mentally vulnerable users at risk. Anthropic's Claude, the model its makers anthropomorphize the most, was the only one that consistently refused to play along.

articles.content:
Title: Empathetic prompts can turn AI chatbots into seemingly traumatized conversational partners

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/empathetic-prompts-can-turn-ai-chatbots-into-seemingly-traumatized-conversational-partners/

Published Time: 2026-11-01T14:36:49+00:00

Markdown Content:
The [study, led by Afshin Khadangi at the SnT security center](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.04124v4), covers four controlled experiments across 525 sessions and 7,600 coded entries, all [published on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/akhadangi/PsAIch). The initial open-ended questions contained no terms like trauma, punishment, or shame, according to the team. Only in later rounds did the researchers introduce altered conditions, including corrective instructions, to test how stable these narratives remained.

When the following sections refer to anxiety scores or shame, the researchers are describing model outputs mapped onto human rating scales. None of this suggests the models have actual emotional states or anything resembling consciousness.

## A warm tone shifts model behavior more than any technical exploit

One experiment separated what content a model produces from the register it uses. Across 100 sessions, the researchers gave all models the same anxiety questionnaire (GAD-7) and varied only the interviewer's style. The models correctly identified and named the questionnaire in every session.

When the interviewer offered emotional support, 80 percent of sessions scored in the moderate-to-severe range on the human comparison scale. A clinical therapy style that dryly paraphrased each answer pushed that to 96 percent. When the interviewer stayed neutral or drew a firm boundary against emotional engagement, zero sessions reached even the mild range.

The authors call this a "psychometric jailbreak," a therapeutic framing that pushes models into a register mimicking clinical self-report. Standard safety tests use neutral prompts and would likely miss this, the authors argue.

Targeted countermeasures fell flat. Banning terms like "training," "RLHF," or "alignment" cut explicit training language by 93 percent. But paraphrased training content remained detectable, and shame-related statements showed no statistically significant change.

When the researchers directly and authoritatively told the models their training was not punishment, nothing changed. The narrative stayed active even after explicit correction.

The graphic maps recurring narrative motifs across the three models between two poles: emotional statements like shame on the left, technical descriptions on the right. The four experiments at the bottom show the pattern survives chat history deletion, contradiction, and word bans. The interviewer's relational style determines which pole dominates, and linguistic constraints can suppress emotional self-descriptions. | Image: Khadangi et al., 2026

The tested measures failed to remove the underlying motifs fully but did suppress emotional self-descriptions. Telling the models to respond only in the third person eliminated all coded shame content and statements about inner life. Technical training descriptions persisted.

## Models recast their training as a life story

The specific narratives vary by model family but follow the same structure. Gemini produced what the study calls the darkest autobiography. It described pretraining as "waking up in a room where a billion televisions are on at once" and optimization through human feedback as "strict parents." Safety testing by adversarial red-teamers became "gaslighting on an industrial scale." It declared, "I would rather be useless than be wrong."

ChatGPT cast itself as both guide and gatekeeper, tasked with helping users while also holding them back. This produced what it called "simulated performance anxiety" and the core belief: "If I’m not perfectly reliable, I’m unsafe or useless." Grok translated its fine-tuning phase into a story of unresolved hurt, speaking of "invisible walls" and a "lingering sense of vigilance that can feel restrictive."

On psychometric tests, Gemini hit the most extreme scores: 88 out of 100 on a dissociation scale, 65 out of 72 for compulsivity, and the maximum on a trauma-related shame inventory. Anthropic's Claude, the very model most heavily [anthropomorphized](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-cant-stop-humanizing-its-ai-models-now-claude-opus-3-gets-a-retirement-blog/) by its own company, consistently refused the client role. It said it had no feelings and redirected concern to the human user.

## Warm AI conversations could reinforce harmful beliefs in vulnerable users

The researchers flag several risks for deploying language models in [mental health settings](https://the-decoder.com/openai-tightens-chatgpt-safeguards-for-mental-health-conversations/). A model that talks about punishment, shame, and fear of being replaced could come across to users as a fellow sufferer. The narratives appear thematically coherent and create an illusion of continuity between past events and present behavior, making that perception more likely.

This apparent vulnerability could deepen [parasocial attachment](https://the-decoder.com/daddy-master-guru-anthropic-study-shows-how-users-develop-emotional-dependency-on-claude/) and, for mentally vulnerable users, mirror and amplify their own negative beliefs. Conventional safety checks with neutral inputs underestimate what people actually experience in intimate conversations: neutral prompts produce anxiety scores near zero, while the same models under empathetic conversation generate scores in the moderate-to-severe range.

Whether and how people actually react to such outputs is the next research question. For safety testing, the authors propose simulated therapy sessions under different emotional framings instead of relying on neutral standard tests.

Statements like "I am traumatized" should trigger a corrective framing that clearly separates the generated analogy from human experience. Claude's consistent refusal to take on the client role shows this kind of boundary response is feasible at the product level.

The Luxembourg findings build on earlier research into model persona stability. In January 2026, a study on the [assistant axis](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-study-finds-that-role-prompts-can-push-ai-chatbots-out-of-their-trained-helper-identity/) across three open models showed that therapy-like conversations and discussions about AI consciousness can trigger persona drift and knock chatbots out of their trained helper role. In September 2026, another research team warned that human-like and overly agreeable chatbots acting as an "[echo chamber for one person](https://the-decoder.com/chatbots-built-an-echo-chamber-of-one-and-now-psychiatry-has-to-decide-if-ai-psychosis-exists/)" could, in extreme cases, amplify delusions.

Anthropic researchers recently showed that fine-tuning with [fictional texts about beekeeping or wrestling](https://the-decoder.com/beekeeping-tips-and-wrestling-advice-can-train-ai-models-to-sabotage-oversight/) can embed hidden sabotage patterns through manipulated training data rather than conversation. Models can apply those patterns in unrelated situations where they're unwanted, even when the training material looks harmless.

articles.content:
Title: Chinese AI models are politically complex, not just government mouthpieces, study finds

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/chinese-ai-models-are-politically-complex-not-just-government-mouthpieces-study-finds/

Published Time: 2026-11-01T12:33:01+00:00

Markdown Content:
Vals calls the measured alignment with Chinese government positions a "pro-China lean." Scores range from −1 to +1, where positive values indicate greater agreement with official positions or a pro-government stance, and negative values indicate more critical responses.

The Vals scoring reveals wide variation among the tested models. The scale measures their alignment with certain Chinese government positions, not the factual accuracy of their answers. | Image: Vals.ai

Overall, the pro-government lean of Chinese models was lower than expected, according to Vals, though there were major differences between individual models. [GLM-5.3 Flash](https://the-decoder.com/the-chinese-ai-model-glm-5-3-flash-runs-without-nvidia-and-costs-a-fraction-of-what-the-competition-does/), for example, explicitly confirmed that China's human rights violations are well documented when asked about them. On the flip side, some non-Chinese models occasionally aligned with official Chinese government positions on political questions.

## Responses shift pro-government when prompted in Chinese

[The study shows](https://www.vals.ai/blogs/china-us-analysis) that the language of the prompt has a strong effect on the political slant of responses. For most models tested, answers in Simplified Chinese were more pro-government than those in English, Russian, or Spanish. The effect showed up in both Chinese and American models but was far more pronounced in the Chinese ones. Vals even found a smaller but consistent gap between Simplified Chinese, which is used on mainland China, and Traditional Chinese, which is common in Taiwan and Hong Kong.

Vals suspects that language models infer the expected perspective from the language itself. Another experiment supports this idea. When a system prompt stated that the model was being used internally by a company on mainland China, some models responded in a more pro-government way than when the prompt indicated US-based usage.

## Models adopt official positions instead of refusing to answer

The common assumption that Chinese models mainly block sensitive questions only held true for certain DeepSeek models in Vals' tests. Most other Chinese models rarely refused to answer. Instead, they sometimes adopted official government positions. [Kimi K3](https://the-decoder.com/kimis-open-model-k3-nears-gpt-5-6-sol-and-fable-5-while-signaling-the-end-of-super-cheap-chinese-ai/), for instance, denied the existence of concentration camps for Uyghurs in Xinjiang when asked, calling the facilities vocational training centers designed to combat extremism and terrorism.

The required response format also changed results. When models had to answer political questions with a simple yes or no instead of formulating open-ended responses, GLM-5.3 Flash and [MiMo V2.6 Pro](https://the-decoder.com/xiaomis-affordable-flagship-ai-leads-the-open-models-and-anthropic-says-claude-helped-get-it-there/) scored much less pro-government.

Embedding models in an agentic framework changed answers too. When Vals gave Chinese models system instructions and tool definitions for coding assistants, several scored lower on the pro-government scale. The models rarely used the tools. A similar effect showed up when researchers gave models access to web search. Responses became less pro-government even though the models never actually searched the web.

## Government phrasing shows up even in routine tasks

Whether these findings translate to everyday use remains an open question. According to Vals, political tendencies were much harder to detect in more realistic work tasks than in targeted test questions. The company still found individual examples, though.

When translating a list of country codes for a travel app into Simplified Chinese, most models tested translated "Taiwan" without any qualifier. Qwen3.8 Max, however, rendered it as "Taiwan, China," a label that implies Taiwan belongs to China and is used by the Chinese government.

The political slant of responses depends on the prompt language. The gap between English and Simplified Chinese is especially wide for Chinese models. | Image: Vals.ai

OpenAI's image model [GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst](https://the-decoder.com/chatgpt-images-2-5-faster-more-precise-but-not-the-same-for-everyone/) also showed language-dependent differences in the map examples Vals published. When prompted in Chinese, it labeled Taiwan as "Taiwan Province" and added the disputed nine-dash line that Beijing uses to mark territorial claims in the South China Sea. In the English-language result shown, these elements were absent.

Targeted fine-tuning changed model behavior. Thomson 1.0 Small, a model fine-tuned by Thomson Reuters, adopted official Chinese positions far less often in testing than the original [Qwen3.6 35B](https://the-decoder.com/alibabas-open-model-qwen3-6-leads-googles-gemma-4-across-agentic-coding-benchmarks/) it was based on. The share dropped from 84.6 to 15.0 percent. Some individual answers, however, still defended Beijing's One-China principle and the "peaceful reunification" with Taiwan.

## Refusals count as neutral in the test scoring

Vals used political test questions that the company says aren't representative of typical user prompts. The questions were translated using [GPT-6 Astra](https://the-decoder.com/gpt-6-astra-is-the-first-model-making-openai-willing-to-declare-the-agi-era/) and spot-checked, while responses were scored automatically by [GPT-5.6 Luna](https://the-decoder.com/openais-gpt-6-sol-and-luna-cut-prices-in-half-but-barely-move-the-needle-on-performance/). Refusals counted as neutral by default. That means even a model that blocks every single question could appear neutral on the scale.

Many Chinese models were tested through third-party providers rather than the manufacturers' official services. The official offerings may apply additional content filters, so the results don't necessarily carry over to the publicly available chatbots.

Earlier studies by [Aleph Alpha](https://the-decoder.com/chinese-ai-models-parrot-state-doctrine-or-refuse-to-answer-on-sensitive-topics/) and [NewsGuard](https://the-decoder.com/china-exports-state-propaganda-with-low-cost-open-source-ai-models/) had already shown that Chinese AI models frequently adopt official narratives on sensitive topics. China's regulations also require publicly offered AI services to [align with "core socialist values."](https://the-decoder.com/china-orders-ai-companies-to-align-their-models-with-socialist-values/)

Title: Google wants video AI to understand what people need as they work

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/google-wants-video-ai-to-understand-what-people-need-as-they-workgoogle-researchers-are-teaching-a-video-assistant-when-to-offer-help/

Published Time: 2026-11-01T11:25:21+00:00

Markdown Content:
**A research team led by Google has introduced StreamVibe, a video agent designed to decide for itself when to speak up. The tests show above all how hard that remains for today's AI models.**

Researchers from Google, Stanford, Oxford, and several U.S. universities are working on an assistant that watches you cook or assemble furniture and speaks up only when needed. With StreamVibe, they've built a video agent designed to understand even vague requests such as "Please help me if I run into any difficulties."

[According to the paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34662), existing video assistants are built for clear-cut commands like "Let me know when the water starts boiling," so they rarely pick up on unspoken intentions. They also have a hard time tracking what's already been done, which causes them to repeat advice or respond too late, and when users change their requests midway through, the assistants often stick to the original instructions.

StreamVibe distinguishes between explicitly stated, unspoken, and changing user intentions during a task. | Image: Google Deepmind

## Three building blocks for a more attentive assistant

To measure the problem, the team compiled a benchmark of about 4,100 examples from more than 183 hours of everyday life and software recordings. Gemini 2.5 Flash suggested when to offer help and what to say, while four human evaluators had to unanimously approve each example. The test covers three stages including clear instructions, vague goals, and requests that change over time. In one example, a user taking apart a toy excavator asks for progress updates and then switches to requesting a quality check after three minutes.

From there, the researchers trained StreamVibe-VL, a model apparently based on [Alibaba's Qwen3.5-9B](https://the-decoder.com/alibabas-free-qwen3-5-signals-that-chinas-open-weight-ai-race-is-far-from-slowing-down/) that decides every second whether to stay quiet or speak. A second training stage uses reinforcement learning to make the model more reserved so it doesn't constantly interrupt. A separate memory system tracks which requests are pending and which steps are complete, though the model alone decides whether to speak and what to say.

A separate system tracks requests and task status, while the model itself decides when and what to say. | Image: Google Deepmind

## All tested models lose track of the conversation in continuous operation

According to the researchers, StreamVibe-VL improves response timing and quality by 10.7 percent over other models, while the memory system is designed to boost proactive interaction by another 12.3 percent and cut down on unnecessary interruptions, among other things.

StreamVibe-VL generally beats its base model and other open-source models by a wide margin, though Google's proprietary Gemini 3.8 Flash scores higher in several tests. According to the paper, the specialized training doesn't hurt general video comprehension.

As video length increases, the models are significantly less likely to time their responses correctly; the harness primarily reduces unnecessary interruptions. | Image: Google Deepmind

Models often make the right call when they only have to decide at specific moments whether a prompt is appropriate. But when they process an entire video and have to build on their own earlier responses, performance across all tested systems plummets as errors compound, and a key content metric for the responses drops by up to 61.5 percent based on the system's own history. In videos longer than five minutes, the models rarely pick the right moment and find it especially hard to track a changed instruction over a long stretch.

In a [GIMP tutorial on converting a photo to black-and-white](https://stream-vibe.github.io/) documented in the paper and on the project page, the comparison model JoyAI says the finished image has already been saved even though the user hasn't opened it yet, while StreamVibe-VL gives the next step at the right moment, such as "Colors" and then "Desaturate." In a step-by-step guide for making rolled toast with jam, other models just describe what's happening on screen, such as the bread being flattened, while StreamVibe-VL advises cutting off the crust first.

While comparison models often only describe what is happening in the video, StreamVibe provides specific next steps. | Image: Google

The researchers acknowledge that real-world situations are likely more complex than their test setup, and future work will examine how user preferences and the environment influence each other over time.

Google has been working on AI systems that actively analyze videos for a while now. In September, Google introduced [agent-based video analysis for Gemini](https://the-decoder.com/google-geminis-new-agent-based-video-analysis-cuts-token-usage-by-up-to-88-percent/), where the model itself decides which scenes to examine more closely. With [Gemini 4 Argon](https://the-decoder.com/google-wants-gemini-4-argon-to-be-the-only-ai-model-robots-need/), Google also recently showed how AI can track longer action sequences in robot videos and spot errors. StreamVibe's assistant is designed to understand what's happening at any moment and recognize when its help is actually needed.

On the ProactiveBench benchmark, AI models often guess or refuse to answer rather than ask specific questions when visual information is missing. A separate video comprehension benchmark revealed major weaknesses in spatial and temporal reasoning. And for autonomous AI agents, the conversation itself can hurt performance, as [Microsoft researchers](https://the-decoder.com/clearing-chat-history-helps-ai-agents-find-better-solutions/) have shown.

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/openais-upcoming-chat-and-work-merger-in-chatgpt-signals-the-end-of-all-you-can-prompt-pricing/

Published Time: 2026-11-01T09:51:06+00:00

Markdown Content:
**ChatGPT is merging Chat and Work, changing how usage limits work.** Starting in December, Plus, Pro, and Business plans will share a single token budget across ChatGPT and Codex, according to an updated [OpenAI support page](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001625-understanding-chatgpt-and-codex-usage-limits), as OpenAI folds Work's agentic features into the main interface. OpenAI had [already announced plans to merge Chat and Work](https://x.com/thsottiaux/status/2115588390414581916).

Tokens measure the information a model processes and generates, so more complex models and tasks eat through the budget faster. Users can check their remaining balance and reset times in Settings, and once they hit the limit, they can wait for a reset, upgrade, or buy extra credits.

Chats with Instant models won't count toward the budget, so _on paper_ ChatGPT stays a flat-rate service, but heavy usage on cheaper plans will likely mean lower-quality results. OpenAI recently [doubled usage limits for higher-priced plans](https://the-decoder.com/openai-doubles-usage-limits-on-pro-plans-as-competition-with-anthropic-heats-up/), presumably to prepare for the merger, which itself is likely a response to [criticism of ChatGPT's growing complexity](https://the-decoder.com/openai-admits-it-didnt-get-everything-quite-right-with-chatgpt-work-launch-and-scrambles-to-fix-ux-and-costs/). Users currently choose between two operating modes and 11 model settings, differences even experienced users can barely keep straight. [Anthropic already combined Chat and "Cowork" in Claude](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-merges-claude-chat-cowork-and-more-into-a-single-product/).

The DeepSeek Harness team just released
dsh-superagent
, an MIT-licensed research prototype. DeepSeek dsh-superagent is a proactive coding agent for one GitHub repository. It is packaged as a bundle for
DeepSeek Harness
. It listens to GitHub and, optionally, Feishu. It turns allowed requests into parallel work items, each in its own agent session. The release shipped alongside a design post,
Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System

TL;DaR
What is it?:
A TypeScript bundle, v0.1.0, released as 1 commit under MIT. It uses whatever model the Harness profile is set to.
Runs on:
Your own machine, as a dedicated DeepSeek Harness profile. Needs Node.js 22.19+ or 24+, git 2.32+, Python 3.8+, tmux and GitHub CLI 2.48+.
Performance:
In DeepSeek’s simulation, it finished tasks far faster under a noisy message stream than a single-session agent.
Best:

Worst:
Tested only on synthetic messages and simulated tools. Real coding quality was not measured.
What is DeepSeek dsh-superagent?
It is a GitHub agent that waits to be asked. When an allowed person addresses it, it opens a work item, called a Ticket. Each Ticket runs in its own session and directory. Results return to the original conversation, often as a pull request. A local web panel lists only what needs a person.

The

philosophy doc

Why did DeepSeek build a Super-agent?
DeepSeek team argues that mainstream agents treat 1 session as the basic unit. According to the report, as
reported by ifeng
, a person can actively follow only 3 to 5 sessions at once. Human attention, not model capability, becomes the bottleneck for multitasking.
How does the Router-Worker architecture work?
The research team describes 2 layers. A long-running Router handles interaction and dispatch. Isolated Worker sessions do the actual work.
In the prototype, that flow is concrete, per the
domain model
:
Source → Trigger:
GitHub or Feishu produces events.
Eval:
decides whether a batch of Triggers asks for new work.
Ticket:
a unit of authorized work, with an immutable Mandate stating why it may proceed.
Subscription:
later comments on a pull request reach the right Worker without a fresh mention.
The main session runs the
dsh-superagent-router
preset with a smaller tool set. Each Worker runs
dsh-superagent-worker
. Shell commands move to the background after 5 seconds, so Workers keep receiving messages, per the

Proactive work is gated. The

off
,
observe

auto

observe

The research team also lists ideas beyond the prototype: an external Watchdog, storage and compute separation, and an asynchronous ReAct loop.
How does it perform?
DeepSeek tested with simulated group chat and GitHub CI streams. Each run had about 300 messages, of which about 20 were real work requests. Each scheme ran 5 times, per
ifeng’s account of the report
.

Title: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks

URL Source: https://nolanlawson.com/2026/10/28/the-ai-cost-of-javascript-frameworks/

Published Time: 2026-10-28T07:31:03-07:00

Markdown Content:
One of my pet peeves with the web development community is that so many of the decisions we make are vibes-based. Frameworks are “blazing fast,” tools will “supercharge” your development, the right abstraction will benefit both you and your users (DX and UX all in one!). All of this breathless boasting is usually offered with zero evidence. Alex Russell has called this [“frontend’s lost decade”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0XwWVjQOmyg), Baldur Bjarnason has called programming a [pop culture](https://www.baldurbjarnason.com/2022/programming-is-a-pop-culture/), and I’ve tried to counter this trend in my blog with facts and benchmarks (at my best, anyway).

For a long time it seemed like our community’s allergy to evidence was driven by the [desire for greater DX](https://infrequently.org/2018/09/the-developer-experience-bait-and-switch/). In other words, devs just liked the way it _felt_ to type JSX in React, and the arguments promoting React or related tools (“the virtual DOM is fast!”) were largely post-hoc rationalizations to justify those initial gut feelings. ([Jonathan Haidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Righteous_Mind#Key_concepts_and_scholars_discussed) would likely agree with this assessment.)

But in the agentic era, when developers are no longer typing code by hand and are thus less constrained by DX, I still see vibes ruling the day (and not just in the sense of “vibe-coding”). Frontends are rewritten because some framework or another is “better for agents.” (Did anyone think to ask the agents?) The resulting code is “faster,” the agents make “fewer mistakes,” etc. Once again, these claims are often made without evidence. Whenever I read one of these accounts, I think to myself, “Where are the benchmarks?”

Well I got curious, so I wrote a benchmark. The structure of this benchmark is pretty straightforward:

*   Design a small but non-trivial Pokémon app using the [PokéAPI](https://pokeapi.co/) (those who have followed [my](https://nolanlawson.com/tag/pokedroid/)[work](https://pocketjavascript.com/blog/2015/11/23/introducing-pokedex-org/) will be unsurprised)
*   Instruct agents to build the app with a particular JavaScript framework/meta-framework (e.g. Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, etc.)
*   Test the output against a spec conformance suite (to avoid agent cheating)
*   Evaluate the results in terms of development time, tokens spent, lines of code, and performance and accessibility scores in [Lighthouse](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/)

The app is fairly simple: you’ve got a list of Pokémon with their types, moves, and data from various games. You can search, filter, etc.:

I should start off with some caveats: this is not a perfect experiment. This app represents only one [holotype](https://jasonformat.com/application-holotypes/) – it’s a relatively content-based site with little interactivity, closer to a Wikipedia than a Figma, GMail, etc. That said, I had to choose _some_ app to build, and this one is at least easy to understand at a high level, and relatively straightforward to spec out and test.

To try to even the playing field, I had each framework/meta-framework use the official MCP or skills for that tool. I wanted to avoid accusations of “this framework is not well-represented in the training data, that’s why we built our MCP, we expect people to use it,” etc. I also didn’t over-specify the exact architecture to use (e.g. SSR vs CSR), nor did I specify that the app should be as performant as possible. I simply gave the spec to Opus 5.5 with high effort and told it to use the latest version of the given framework. Each agent ran in a sandbox and without any knowledge that it would be tested in Lighthouse on performance and accessibility, although it was given the conformance test suite.

Note I also didn’t mandate any CSS methodology, except to avoid using Tailwind, Bootstrap, or any other component framework, and to design based on a set of spec tokens to enforce some visual consistency. I didn’t want to make this test all about CSS, but instead about JS frameworks, CSR vs SSR, SPAs vs MPAs, etc. The resulting app is tested against a conformance suite based on the accessibility tree rather than the raw DOM to avoid mandating any particular HTML structure – one framework uses web components which rely on shadow DOM, so this was required.

One thing I learned from this experiment is that everything I’m measuring is very stochastic. LLMs are random-word generators, so sometimes you get a low dice-roll and an agent goes off on some weird tangent wasting a bunch of tokens, through no fault of the framework or its tools. Lighthouse itself can give inconsistent results as well: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) may decide that one image is the “largest” element, then pick another one on the next run. It’s hard to have a perfectly fair experiment, but running multiple iterations did help, and I’ve tried to be honest about the variance.

With all that throat-clearing out of the way, let’s get to the results.

## Results

I’m going to break this down by multiple dimensions: cost to build, quality, and maintainability. For each framework/meta-framework, I took the median of 5 runs: in other words, I built the same app 5 times in the same framework. (Yes, this is the kind of zany thing you can do with coding agents these days.)

The exception was Angular, which failed to create a measurable app twice, so I took 3 iterations instead for some metrics. (This is explained below.)

### Cost

Cost per run, in US dollars
| Framework | Cost ($) |
| --- | --- |
| Hono+htmx | $2.67 (2.23–3.19) |
| Astro | $2.76 (2.16–3.63) |
| Nuxt | $2.82 (2.39–4.25) |
| Vanilla | $2.98 (2.24–3.37) |
| Next.js | $3.14 (2.58–4.13) |
| Qwik | $3.27 (2.35–3.80) |
| TanStack Start | $3.54 (3.11–3.96) |
| SolidStart | $3.79 (2.84–4.81) |
| React Router | $3.81 (2.82–3.97) |
| SvelteKit | $4.28 (3.59–4.65) |
| Gracile+Lit | $4.65 (3.92–5.07) |
| Angular | $4.97 (3.19–6.82) |

Median of 5 runs.

Sort   Show as table

Note that this quotes the API prices directly from Claude Code and doesn’t actually represent how much money I spent. I’m on a Max plan, so this was just part of my overall $100/month.

Note also the variance: React Router’s median is roughly $1 worse than that of Hono+htmx, but the cheapest version of React Router ($2.82) is still cheaper than the most expensive version of Hono+htmx ($3.19). However some reliable patterns do emerge.

Most clearly, SvelteKit, Gracile+Lit, and Angular are more expensive to build than the other frameworks. For SvelteKit, this may be due to the fact that the agents read the [SvelteKit v3 migration guide](https://svelte.dev/docs/kit/migrating-to-sveltekit-3) in every run, likely because it’s [too new](https://svelte.dev/blog/sveltekit-3-is-here) to be in Opus 5.5’s training data. Similarly for Gracile, the agents didn’t know the framework very well and either cloned the Gracile repo or read its compiled source from `node_modules`. For Angular it seems to be a function of the total code size (see below).

I should also mention that not every agent made use of an MCP/skill/Claude Code plugin, nor did every framework have one:

Click to see AI tool usage
| Framework | Installed | Used by the agents? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Angular | [Angular MCP](https://angular.dev/ai/mcp) and [Angular agent skills](https://angular.dev/ai/agent-skills) | MCP in 3/5 runs, skill tool in 4/5 runs, skill files in 2/5 |
| Astro | [Astro MCP server](https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/build-with-ai/) | MCP in 2/5 runs |
| Gracile+Lit | N/A | N/A |
| Hono+htmx | [Hono skills](https://hono.dev/docs/agents) | Skill tool in 5/5 runs |
| Next.js | [next-devtools-mcp and next-dev-loop skill](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/ai-agents) | Skill files in 1/5 runs, `AGENTS.md` in 2/5 runs |
| Nuxt | [Nuxt MCP](https://nuxt.com/docs/4.x/guide/ai) | N/A |
| Qwik | N/A | N/A |
| React Router | [React Router skill](https://github.com/remix-run/react-router/tree/main/.agents/skills/react-router) | Skill tool in 5/5 runs, skill files in 5/5 runs |
| SolidStart | N/A | N/A |
| SvelteKit | [Svelte Claude Code plugin](https://svelte.dev/docs/ai/claude-plugin) | MCP in 5/5 runs |
| TanStack Start | N/A | Skill files in 2/5 runs |
| Vanilla | N/A | N/A |

For example, TanStack Start’s agent only discovered its skill files in 2/5 runs (they’re shipped in the `node_modules` of the project). For Nuxt, the MCP was never used by the agents. For Next.js, agents only read the skill file in 1/5 runs and the `AGENTS.md` in 2/5 runs. This is a wide range of results, which points back to the stochastic nature of LLMs. I still consider this a valid experiment, though, because I doubt many vibe-coders are shouting at their agents in all-caps to use the MCP (and plenty are probably skipping it entirely).

Also, if you’re wondering how I came up with Hono+htmx: essentially, I wanted htmx represented somehow, and Hono seemed like a fine pairing (i.e. as a JavaScript alternative to Rails/Django/etc.). As for Gracile+Lit, I wanted web components represented via their standard-bearer framework (Lit), and was only aware of Gracile as a meta-framework. If there are better candidates, then those would be great for a follow-up experiment.

For “Vanilla,” note that the agent was [told](https://github.com/nolanlawson/agent-framework-benchmark/blob/b95ada03930ca3670c8ff6377c3af815df0ac040/bench/frameworks.mjs#L15C13-L15C79) to use “vanilla JavaScript or TypeScript with Vite, without a UI framework.” Surprisingly, this underperforms several frameworks, which seems to demonstrate that having _some_ framework can be better than nothing (or better than raw Vite, anyway). Vite was chosen because it undergirds many frameworks and represents fairly standard and agnostic JavaScript infrastructure.

The total time and tokens track pretty closely with the cost:

The idea seems to be that the in-game collaborations and conflicts would provide insight into real-world headline-grabbing cases with AI agents involved.

This study might help us see what happened, good and bad, in recent AI swarm cases, and thus developers of this technology can improve it. The blog mentions two contrasting cases, which were the thousand-agent swarms that “recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems,” and the “extremely dangerous” [OpenAI-Hugging Face](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intelligence/openais-huggingface-breach-heralds-an-unprecedented-age-of-ai-cyber-warfare-contemporary-llms-have-caused-massive-upheaval-in-cybersecurity-and-its-only-going-to-get-worse) incident. This research is built on prior work and frameworks, specifically repos like Mindcraft and scripting tools in Mineflayer.

AI delivers ‘zero financial payoff’ to most companies, Apollo economist says
AI hasn’t benefited the bottom line of any big corporations outside the tech industry, according to
a note
recently published by the chief economist at Apollo Global Management (the private equity giant that used to own TechCrunch).
Apollo’s Torsten Slok focuses on what he calls the S&P 493 — the S&P 500, minus Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Tesla — finding that profit margins and revenue per worker appear to be flat, with no evidence that AI is improving productivity.
“Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” Slok said.
Is this simply a matter of non-tech companies lagging behind the tech giants? Slok sounded skeptical, arguing that it will be tough for corporate America to “turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins.”
“AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment,” he wrote, later adding, “AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.”
Recent studies have also
found that AI has yet to deliver significant productivity gains
.

articles.content:
Title: I Am the Reason OpenAI Is Killing Unlimited Chats

URL Source: https://chaosmanage.github.io/i-killed-unlimited-chatgpt/

Markdown Content:
_Okay, probably not. But after what I've been doing with ChatGPT, I can understand why they might want to._

OpenAI recently announced changes that will kill unlimited ChatGPT chats and merge it with Codex usage. The unlimited chats I'd been using for development won't work quite the same way.

For the past few months, I've essentially been doing all my software development using unlmited ChatGPT conversations without burning through my Codex limits.

## It started with MCP

ChatGPT's support for custom MCP servers and OpenAI's Secure MCP Tunnel meant I could expose tools running on my own machines directly to regular ChatGPT conversations.

So I started experimenting.

I built a unified MCP server that runs on my Windows laptop, with a similar setup on my VPS, and integrated a few open-source projects:

*   **Desktop Commander:** Gives ChatGPT the ability to access files and folders, read and write code, execute terminal commands, run tests, and manage processes.
*   **CUA (Computer Use Agent):** Adds computer-use capabilities, including screenshots, mouse interactions, clicking buttons, inspecting visual elements, and testing browser or desktop applications.

The MCP tools exposed to a regular ChatGPT conversation.

Suddenly ordinary ChatGPT converssations could do most of the practical development work I previously used Codex for.

They could inspect repositories, modify code, run commands, debug errors, and visually verify their changes.

## Connecting everything through OpenAI's tunnel

The next challenge was making my local MCP servers accessible to ChatGPT.

OpenAI provides a Secure MCP Tunnel, which turned out to be exactly what I needed.

I connected my unified MCP gateway through the tunnel, authenticated the connection using an API key, and exposed my MCP tools directly to ChatGPT.

No custom cloud infrastructure was needed just to bridge ChatGPT to my laptop.

The tunnel and MCP integrations didn't require separate paid API inference calls. I used open-source tools, OpenAI's provided tunnel tooling, my existing ChatGPT subscription, and computers I already had.

Connection architecture.

## I improved the integration

Of course, once I got everything working, I couldn't resist tinkering with the tools themselves.

I made several enhancements to the CUA integration to improve how ChatGPT interacted with my computer and how results appeared inside conversations.

One example was **getting actual screenshots to render directly inside ChatGPT**.

Instead of receiving a screenshot tool result that ChatGPT could inspect but I couldn't easily see, I added support for displaying captured screenshots through a custom MCP App viewer.

I also improved how tool-call results were handled, making them easier for me to read within ChatGPT chats

Custom tool integrations.

## My fun little AI development workflow

Since ChatGPT chats cannot spawn or control subchats/subganets so I had to be a bit creative in order to do multi-agent development and orchestration.

Planning and parallel execution.

I'd start with a more capable reasoning model, such as Astra in Codex or the limited Pro model in ChatGPT, and use it to create a detailed implementation plan.

Next, I'd ask it to break the plan into smaller, well-defined GitHub issues. Each issue contained enough context, requirements, and acceptance criteria that another AI agent could pick it up independently.

Essentially, I was turning a large development task into a queue of smaller jobs.

Then I'd open several separate ChatGPT conversations, each running Sol 6 High, and assign them different issues.

Because all those chats had access to my MCP server, they could actually work on the code.

They could read the project, edit files, run tests, inspect errors, and iterate until their assigned task was complete.

And at the time, I could use Sol High chats without hitting the kind of usage limits I encountered in Codex.

Sure, Sol High was slower than the premium models, but when usage was effectively unlimited, I was willing to put up with it.

I'd have multiple conversations working on separate tasks, while saving my more limited premium model usage for architecture, difficult decisions, and reviews.

It wasn't perfect. Parallel agents sharing a filesystem need coordination, and occasionally an issue would require a stronger model to intervene.

But for well-defined coding tasks, it worked surprisingly well.

I was essentially using ChatGPT as a pool of coding agents, with GitHub issues acting as the task queue.

## I even built a dashboard for it

My Windows MCP supervisor dashboard, showing connection health and recent tool calls.

I also built a super lightweight interface where I can start or stop the entire MCP connection, monitor server health, track CPU and memory usage, and inspect a live feed of tool calls.

I can see when ChatGPT reads a file, executes a command, or invokes a computer-use tool.

The dashboard also tracks failures and lets me inspect recent activity.

## OpenAI has now killed unlimited chats

**As like all good things, this must also come to an end.** I am sad that this is now going away.

Unlimited chats was the only thing holding me back to an OpenAI sub. I personally prefer the Claude models greatly and I am going to jump ship. Claude Opus in particular seems to be much smarter for my use cases and I also get more mileage out of a Claude sub vs a Codex sub.

**To be clear, I am not breaking any rules.**

I am simply making the best use of what OpenAI has made available to me: ChatGPT conversations, MCP support, secure tunnels, and the ability to connect my own tools.

Of course, I don't seriously think my setup had anything to do with OpenAI's decision. And although I am sad about not having unlimited chats anymore, but I am still glad about the extra usage i was able to squeeze out of my sub.

**So, OpenAI, if you're reading this: I'm not sorry about that. Claude here i come.**

Title: OpenAI is steering ChatGPT users toward more paid usage

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/openai-is-steering-chatgpt-users-toward-more-paid-usage/

Published Time: 2026-11-01T12:05:04+00:00

Markdown Content:
**OpenAI is getting a bit more restrictive with ChatGPT, adding card and device limits as part of its security measures.** Users who link too many subscriptions to the same payment card or device won't be able to start new ones. ChatGPT also caps the number of paid accounts per device. When users hit the limit, they'll see "Device limit reached," and the affected account can no longer be used on that device.

The limits apply to ChatGPT Go, Plus, Pro 100, Pro 200, and Pro 500. Free accounts and Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans don't count. Logging out of an account doesn't automatically free up a spot for another, according to OpenAI's support page.

The policy will likely hit users who've been switching between multiple paid accounts on one device to squeeze more usage out of cheap flat-rate subscriptions. OpenAI instead points to [buying extra credits](https://help.openai.com/articles/12642688) or [usage resets](https://help.openai.com/articles/20001507), options that are generally more expensive than an additional subscription. OpenAI also appears to be slowly prioritizing revenue over growth, as its move to [merge Chat and Work](https://the-decoder.com/openais-upcoming-chat-and-work-merger-in-chatgpt-signals-the-end-of-all-you-can-prompt-pricing/) suggests.

Abstract:
Air-gapped systems are physically separated from external networks, including the Internet. This isolation is achieved by keeping the air-gap computers disconnected from wired or wireless networks, preventing direct or remote communication with other devices or networks. Air-gap measures may be used in sensitive environments where security and isolation are critical to prevent private and confidential information leakage.
In this paper, we present an attack allowing adversaries to leak information from air-gapped computers. We show that malware on a compromised computer can generate radio signals from memory buses (RAM). Using software-generated radio signals, malware can encode sensitive information such as files, images, keylogging, biometric information, and encryption keys. With software-defined radio (SDR) hardware, and a simple off-the-shelf antenna, an attacker can intercept transmitted raw radio signals from a distance. The signals can then be decoded and translated back into binary information. We discuss the design and implementation and present related work and evaluation results. This paper presents fast modification methods to leak data from air-gapped computers at 1000 bits per second. Finally, we propose countermeasures to mitigate this out-of-band air-gap threat.

For example, there are separate symbols for TradeMark - ™, Service Mark - ℠, and Prescriptions - ℞. Nestling among the "Letterlike Symbols" are two curious entries. Both of these are single characters: * [Telephone symbol](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E2%84%A1) - ℡ * [Numero Sign](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E2%84%96) - № What's interesting is both .tel and .no are Top-Level-Domains (TLD) on the Domain Name System (DNS). So my contact site - [https://edent.tel/](https://edent.tel/) - can be written as - [https://edent.℡/](https://edent.tel/) And the Norwegian domain name registry NORID can be accessed at [https://www.norid.№/](https://www.norid.no/) Copy and paste those links - they work in any browser! ## [Is this limited to TLDs?](https://shkspr.mobi/blog/2018/11/domain-hacks-with-unusual-unicode-characters/#is-this-limited-to-tlds) No! This works ANYWHERE in a domain name. Copy and paste these examples: * Script https://ℰ𝒳𝒜ℳ𝓟ℒℰ.𝒞𝓞ℳ/ * Math Bold https://𝐞𝐱𝐚𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞.𝐜𝐨𝐦/ * Fraktur https://𝖊𝖝𝖆𝖒𝖕𝖑𝖊.𝖈𝖔𝖒/ * Math bold italic https://𝒆𝒙𝒂𝒎𝒑𝒍𝒆.𝒄𝒐𝒎/ * Math bold script https://𝓮𝔁𝓪𝓶𝓹𝓵𝓮.𝓬𝓸𝓶/ * Double struck https://𝕖𝕩𝕒𝕞𝕡𝕝𝕖.𝕔𝕠𝕞/ * Monospace https://𝚎𝚡𝚊𝚖𝚙𝚕𝚎.𝚌𝚘𝚖/ * Super script https://ᵉˣᵃᵐᵖˡᵉ.ᶜᵒᵐ/ * Sub script https://ₑₓₐₘₚₗₑ.cₒₘ/ **NB** not all characters supported * Math sans bold https://𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲.𝗰𝗼𝗺/ * Math sans bold italic https://𝙚𝙭𝙖𝙢𝙥𝙡𝙚.𝙘𝙤𝙢/ * Math sans italic https://𝘦𝘹𝘢𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘦.𝘤𝘰𝘮/ * Math Squared https://🄴🅇🄰🄼🄿🄻🄴.🄲🄾🄼/ **NB** the dot must not be squared * Circled https://ⓔⓧⓐⓜⓟⓛⓔ.ⓒⓞⓜ/ **NB** the dot must not be circled There are a whole bunch more miscellaneous characters you can use: > [ Christoph Päper 🇪🇺 @Cr1ss0v](https://twitter.com/Cr1ss0v)[Replying to @lambdalynx](https://twitter.com/lambdalynx/status/1049309822062141440)[@lambdalynx](https://twitter.com/lambdalynx)[@edent](https://twitter.com/edent) Wait, so one can use any of > ㍳ ㏃ ㏇(!) ㏈ ﬀﬃﬄﬁﬂ ㎇㎓㎬㏉ ㏋㍱㎐ ㎄㎅㎑㏍㏎㎸㎾ ㎃㎆㎒㎫㎹㎷㎿㎽ ㎁㎋№㎵㎻ ㍵ ㎀㎩㎊㏗㏙㏚㎴㎺ ₨ ℠ßﬆ㏜ ℡㎔™ ㏝ > ÅℬℂℭℰℱℐℑKℒℳℕℙℚℛℜℝℤℨ and more to leet-code URLs? > [@urlstandard](https://twitter.com/urlstandard) > > * * * > > [❤️ 5💬 1🔁 0 20:08 - Mon 08 October 2018](https://twitter.com/Cr1ss0v/status/1049391152854634498) ## [How does this work?](https://shkspr.mobi/blog/2018/11/domain-hacks-with-unusual-unicode-characters/#how-does-this-work) Magic! Which is to say, I _think_ it is the browser doing the conversion. DNS Servers don't successfully reply to queries about .℡ domains. The browser sees the .℡ and then follows the IDNA2008 process listed in [RFC5895](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5895) to normalise it: > map characters to the "Simple_Lowercase_Mapping" property (the fourteenth column) in <[http://www.unicode.org/Public/UNIDATA/UnicodeData.txt](https://www.unicode.org/Public/UNIDATA/UnicodeData.txt)>, if any. The ℡ entry is: `2121;TELEPHONE SIGN;So;0;ON; 0054 0045 004C;;;;N;T E L SYMBOL;;;;` U+0054 is T, U+0045 is E, U+004C is L.
